vignette:
He is 51, South Eastern Asian, married, and has built a life around careful thinking. As a policy analyst, he is used to reading situations, weighing probabilities, and assuming that if he understands enough, he can help prevent harm. Before the storm, that way of living feels like a source of pride. He is the person who checks the forecasts, stores bottled water, and reminds his family to keep passports and documents in one place. He believes preparation can make the world manageable.

The disaster arrives anyway.

A cyclone tears through his coastal town in the middle of the night. He wakes to the sound of the roof shaking and the strange, deep roar of wind that seems to come from everywhere at once. In the dark, he can hear his wife calling his name and the thud of objects hitting the walls. The electricity fails, and the house becomes a confusing black box of movement and noise. He remembers water rising too quickly, muddy and cold around his ankles, then his knees, then his waist. He carries what he can. There is a moment when he thinks he may lose his wife in the chaos, and that thought lands in him with a force he cannot yet name. They escape to higher ground with neighbors, standing in the rain and watching the neighborhood disappear into a moving brown sheet. By morning, the place he knows is unrecognizable.

In the months after, he tries to do what he has always done: gather information, make a plan, be useful. At work, he returns to policy briefs about disaster recovery, infrastructure, and emergency preparedness, but the material feels close enough to his own life that he cannot hold it at a distance. He finds himself staring at lines on a page and realizing he has read the same sentence several times without taking in a word. Colleagues say he is "not himself," quieter than before, slower to join meetings, more likely to sit through lunch without eating. He tells them he is just tired. He means it. He is tired in a way sleep does not fix.

At home, he becomes watchful. He checks the weather many times a day, even when the sky is clear. He avoids the riverfront and the stretch of road where the floodwater had been deepest. When heavy rain starts, his body reacts before his mind can catch up: his chest tightens, his stomach turns, and he feels an urgent need to get moving. He keeps a bag packed near the door. His wife notices that he jumps when a truck passes too loudly or when water splashes in the sink. He is embarrassed by how quickly his heart races, by how his hands tremble when he thinks no one sees.

He does not talk much about what happened. When relatives ask, he gives a careful summary and changes the subject. There are images he cannot explain without feeling foolish or overwhelmed: the look on his wife's face when they first realized the house was taking water, the sound of a child crying in the dark shelter, the sight of furniture floating like abandoned bodies. At night, he wakes from dreams in which he is searching for his family through endless water or trying to speak while mud fills his mouth. Sometimes he wakes already panicked, before the dream becomes clear, his body convinced the storm has returned. He lies still, listening to the house, then gets up to check the windows and locks.

Over time, he notices that joy feels farther away. He still goes to work, still pays bills, still attends to family obligations, but much of life feels reduced to tasks he can complete automatically. He finds it harder to feel connected during gatherings, even with people he loves. His wife tells him he seems present in the room but not entirely there. He recognizes that as true. He sits with others and hears them speak, yet some part of him remains in the flooded dark, waiting for the next wall of water.

He is not reckless, and he is not falling apart in a way others can easily see. From the outside, he may appear composed, even stoic. But inside, the disaster has changed the way he measures safety. Ordinary weather no longer feels ordinary. A distant forecast can ruin his concentration for hours. The body that once trusted routines now stays braced for sudden loss, as if another warning could arrive at any moment.
